edits.old: This subsection asks what FMCW must improve, and by how much, to match ToF's point rate per watt. Three improvements must land together: a cheap, low-power multichannel coherent receiver, more efficient CW lasers and amplifiers, and a lower optical energy per point. **The target.** Parity (§C7a) means ≥15 Mpts/s in ≤15 W at 200 m and 10%. Sensor power is overhead plus point rate times electrical energy per point:
$$P=P_{\rm oh}+\dot N\left(\frac{E_{\rm pt}}{\eta_{\rm wp}}+E_{\rm rx}\right), \tag{122}$$
where $P$ is the sensor's electrical power and $P_{\rm oh}$ the fixed overhead that does not scale with point rate. $\dot N$ is the point rate, $E_{\rm pt}$ the optical energy per point, $\eta_{\rm wp}$ the laser and amplifier wall-plug efficiency (light out per electrical power in), so $E_{\rm pt}/\eta_{\rm wp}$ is the laser's electrical energy per point. $E_{\rm rx}$ is the receiver's electrical energy per point (samples, TIA and bias; subsection 3). With $P_{\rm oh}=3$ W, parity needs
$$\frac{E_{\rm pt}}{\eta_{\rm wp}}+E_{\rm rx}\le\frac{15-3\ {\rm W}}{15\times10^{6}\ {\rm s^{-1}}}=0.8\ \mu{\rm J}. \tag{123}$$
In words: after the overhead, each point may cost at most 0.8 µJ of electricity, for its light and its receiver together. Eq. (122) is Eq. (118) of subsection 2(h) with the dead-time light left out, no coherent loss ($E'=E_{\rm pt}$) and the per-channel receiver terms folded into $E_{\rm rx}$ (Eq. (96)). Subsection 2(h) evaluated Eq. (118) at 10 Mpts/s and 300 m, whereas this subsection evaluates Eq. (122) at 15 Mpts/s and 200 m, so the ≈68 W there and the ≈67 W below are different cases.
edits.new:
**The target.** Parity, in this report, means ≥15 Mpts/s in ≤15 W at 200 m and 10% (§C7a subsection 5 summarizes the conditions derived here). The 2026 SPAD ToF reference of §C7a, at 0.415 µJ of electrical energy per point, meets it with room to spare: $3\ {\rm W}+15\times10^{6}\ {\rm s^{-1}}\times0.415\ \mu{\rm J}=9.2$ W. Sensor power is overhead plus point rate times electrical energy per point:
$$P=P_{\rm oh}+\dot N\left(\frac{E_{\rm pt}}{\eta_{\rm wp}}\,\frac{T_{\rm dwell}}{T_{\rm int}}+E_{\rm rx}\right), \tag{122}$$
where $P$ is the sensor's electrical power and $P_{\rm oh}$ the fixed overhead that does not scale with point rate. $\dot N$ is the point rate, $E_{\rm pt}$ the optical energy per point and $\eta_{\rm wp}$ the laser and amplifier wall-plug efficiency (light out per electrical power in). $T_{\rm dwell}/T_{\rm int}=1+2\tau P_{\rm ch}/E_{\rm pt}$ (Eq. (107)) is the factor by which an ungated CW transmitter emits more than the useful energy: $12.67/10=1.27$ at the §C7a dwell, and 1 for a transmitter switched off during the last $\tau$ of each ramp. The first term in the bracket is therefore the laser's electrical energy per point. $E_{\rm rx}$ is the receiver's electrical energy per point (samples, TIA and bias over the whole dwell; subsection 3). With $P_{\rm oh}=3$ W, parity needs
$$\frac{E_{\rm pt}}{\eta_{\rm wp}}\,\frac{T_{\rm dwell}}{T_{\rm int}}+E_{\rm rx}\le\frac{15-3\ {\rm W}}{15\times10^{6}\ {\rm s^{-1}}}=0.8\ \mu{\rm J}. \tag{123}$$
In words: after the overhead, each point may cost at most 0.8 µJ of electricity, for its light and its receiver together, i.e. $0.8/0.415=1.9$ times what the ToF reference spends per point. Eq. (122) is Eq. (118) of subsection 2(h) with its useful and dead-time light combined in the factor $T_{\rm dwell}/T_{\rm int}$, the per-channel receiver terms folded into $E_{\rm rx}$ (Eq. (96)) and no coherent loss ($E'=E_{\rm pt}$), which holds to within 1 dB for a laser of ≲27 kHz at 200 m (≲55 kHz keeps the loss within 3 dB at 300 m; Eq. (115) and its table). Subsection 2(h) evaluated Eq. (118) at 10 Mpts/s and 300 m, whereas this subsection evaluates Eq. (122) at 15 Mpts/s and 200 m, so the ≈68 W there and the ≈76.5 W below are different cases.

A CW laser transmits for the whole dwell $T_{\rm dwell}$, not just for the useful integration time $T_{\rm int}=E_{\rm pt}/P_{\rm ch}$. The transmitted energy per point is therefore $E_{\rm pt}\,T_{\rm dwell}/T_{\rm int}$ (subsection 1(e)), with $T_{\rm dwell}=T_{\rm int}+2\tau$ from Eq. (107).

- **At 30 mW per channel:** $T_{\rm int}=0.15\ \mu{\rm J}/0.03\ {\rm W}=5$ µs and $T_{\rm dwell}=7.67$ µs, so 15 Mpts/s needs only $15\times10^{6}\times7.67\times10^{-6}=115$ channels.
  - Ungated, each point emits $0.15\times7.67/5=0.230$ µJ, and the total is $0.230/0.30+0.10=0.867$ µJ, i.e. $3+15\times0.867=16.0$ W, above the target.
  - Switched off during the last $\tau$ of each ramp (subsection 2(i), item 2), the transmitter emits only $E_{\rm pt}$: $0.15/0.30+0.10=0.60$ µJ, i.e. $3+15\times0.60=12.0$ W, at any power per channel.
- **The ungated ceiling:** Eq. (123) with $\eta_{\rm wp}=0.30$ and $E_{\rm rx}=0.10$ µJ allows $T_{\rm dwell}/T_{\rm int}\le(0.8-0.10)\times0.30/0.15=1.40$, i.e. $2\tau P_{\rm ch}/E_{\rm pt}\le0.40$, so $P_{\rm ch}\le0.40\times0.15\ \mu{\rm J}/2.67\ \mu{\rm s}=22.5$ mW. Then $T_{\rm int}=0.15\ \mu{\rm J}/22.5\ {\rm mW}=6.67$ µs, and 15 Mpts/s needs $15\times10^{6}\times(6.67+2.67)\times10^{-6}=140$ channels.
- Parity therefore also forces a choice between many dim channels (140–190 at 15–22.5 mW, ungated) and fewer bright ones behind a transmitter switched off during the last $\tau$ of each ramp (115 at 30 mW).

**Do the three conditions still reach parity?** Yes, but narrowly [E].
- Ungated, as in the §C7a model, the "all three" case draws 14.0 W at 15 Mpts/s, 1 W inside the target, and only while each channel carries ≤22.5 mW.
- The receiver condition is the tightest: with the other two met, Eq. (123) leaves $0.8-0.633=0.17$ µJ per point for the receiver, 14× below today's 2.34 µJ.
- Parity in this sense is not equality with ToF. The parity case still spends $0.733/0.415=1.8$ times the electrical energy per point of the 2026 SPAD ToF reference, which delivers the same 15 Mpts/s in 9.2 W. Matching that reference point for point would need, even with a gated transmitter, $\eta_{\rm wp}=0.30$ and a 0.10 µJ receiver, an optical energy of $(0.415-0.10)\times0.30=0.095$ µJ per point. By Eq. (97) that is a receive efficiency near $0.25\times0.303/0.095=0.80$, far above the 0.5 that the parity case already assumes.

**The per-channel budget at parity** follows from these numbers:
- 140–190 channels (560–760 receivers) at ≈15–22.5 mW of optical power each with an ungated transmitter, or 115 channels (460 receivers) at 30 mW with a gated one;
- ≈8–13 mW of receive power per channel, i.e. ≈2–3 mW for each of its four receivers, including ≈1 GS/s ADCs and FFT. This comes from dividing the receiver power $E_{\rm rx}\dot N=0.10\ \mu{\rm J}\times15\times10^{6}\ {\rm s^{-1}}=1.5$ W by the channel count $N_{\rm ch}$: 7.9, 10.7 or 13.0 mW for 190, 140 or 115 channels, and 2.0, 2.7 or 3.3 mW per receiver. Today's §C7a receiver draws ≈46 mW ($2.337\ \mu{\rm J}/12.67\ \mu{\rm s}/4$), 14–23× more.
